prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling atomic clocks and precision measurements at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye) as the sole prize part, and nothing in round 1 moved me off it. The decisive features have not changed: magic-wavelength trapping removes the lattice Stark shift while thousands of neutral atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and the resulting clocks reached fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and have been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories. As an instrument builder I value an invention that opens a new measurement regime and then survives independent replication, and this one does both. The chair's first question, whether the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, is answered in round 1 by Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig on physical grounds: the comb is a readout tool, ion control is a different regime, and neither removes the trapping shift for a many-atom ensemble. I accept that this argument needs to be carried by the citation, so I now want the wording to name the optical lattice clock explicitly and not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general, as Danielsson, Mehlig and Kroll ask. On maturity, I treat the pending SI redefinition of the second as a consequence of settled physics and not as a reason to give or withhold the prize, and I would keep it out of the citation. On credit, a two-name split between concept and performance is the only configuration on the shortlist that needs no forced third name and no contested boundary.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that the lattice clock may read as incremental after 2005 and 2012, and Olsson presses that clean attribution is not the same as scientific consequence. I take that seriously: the clock refines an existing capability, whereas the quantum spin Hall effect opened a class of matter. I judge the consequence of the clock to be real and measurable (relativistic geodesy, tests of constants, new-physics searches), but I cannot show it is larger than that of B007, and I say so. The second objection is credit. Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and other groups are not named, and the committee has not verified from documents the priority sequence between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations. Lindroth, Kroll and I all recall this history from general knowledge, and I would not let the citation assert a priority claim that we cannot support. Third, a prize in a metrology lineage that already has two recent awards could be judged conservative, and a single two-person AMO prize leaves faster-moving fields waiting.

responses.point: Olsson argues that B007 opened a materials class and conceptual framework, that clean attribution is not the same as scientific consequence, and that the BHZ gap is imperfect but not disqualifying.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my configuration and I do not wave it away. I agree that the Z2 invariant is a new organising principle and I accept your point that the 2016 prize is not a bar, since the time-reversal-symmetric helical edge is a different step from the Haldane and Thouless lineage. Where I still differ is on what a prize citation must be able to say. You write that the HgTe proposal gave a concrete platform and the experiment followed it; if so, the observation that the citation would honour is one the credited trio did not originate, and the experiment-side recognition would rest on a proposal by someone who cannot be credited. I cannot call that an imperfection of the same size as the Ludlow and Lemonde tail on the clock, which concerns later implementations of a concept already credited. I also hold that the clock's consequence is not small, since it sets the accuracy frontier for the redefinition of the second. So I keep B007 as my first alternative, and I would be willing to revisit if the committee concluded that BHZ was not indispensable.

responses.point: Eriksson accepts a real unfairness to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang but would keep B007 centred on the concept of Kane and Mele plus the first confirmation, and says the lattice clock extends a metrology line already honoured.
responses.response: Your reply to the chair's question is honest, and I think it is the crux: you would phrase the citation so as not to claim the HgTe proposal. But the citation you propose also credits the experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, and Eriksson notes yourself that BHZ told the experimentalists which thickness to grow. A citation cannot praise the observation and omit the proposal that made it possible without readers asking why. With Zhang's death in 2018 and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan also outside the trio, I judge the boundary harder to defend than the one for the clock. I agree with you that the clock extends a metrology line, but not that the line makes it incremental, since the comb is a tool and the lattice clock removes a specific systematic that limited neutral-atom clocks. I do not change my ordering, but I accept that your argument is why B007 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth says neither she nor Kroll has verified the early priority sequence, wants it checked before citation wording is fixed, and asks whether B003 can show which contributions of Halzen and Karle were decisive.
responses.response: I agree that priority should not be asserted from memory, and I take your request for verification as a condition on the citation, not on the prize. My answer is to draft the citation as for the invention and development of the lattice clock and to avoid wording that divides concept from performance between the two names. The split between Katori and Ye is then my reading of their roles and not a claim the citation makes. On B003 I cannot answer your question from the supplied files: I cannot verify that Halzen's scientific leadership and Karle's role in construction and the discovery analysis are the decisive pair, and I accept your point that source identification is behind the clock in maturity. I therefore no longer present IceCube as a candidate for this year and keep it only as a later-year alternative.

responses.point: Johansson puts B056 together with Hosono's B037 as a second part, arguing both have clean attribution, and concedes that the two parts have almost nothing in common and that Hosono has thin support among colleagues.
responses.response: I accept your conclusion on B056, and I respect that you moved it from sixth to the centre of your configuration. I do not follow you on adding B037. You concede that the two parts share nothing, that Hosono is ranked fourth or lower by the members who ranked him, and that the pairing mechanism is open. A second part chosen chiefly because it uses the third name does not satisfy my criterion that the achievement be what the committee would choose on its own merit. I also note that the clean-attribution argument cuts less for Hosono than you suggest, because the Tc-raising work and the reproduction by other groups followed within months. I would prefer one part now, and if a second part is considered, it should be something that the committee has actually argued for in round 1, and no member beyond you has argued for B037. I would also note that your own conflict disclosure for B058 is the right way to handle that candidate.

responses.point: Kroll says the concept-versus-performance split is partly intertwined historically, would write the citation as an invention and its development, would not widen the credit, and discloses a research stay in Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with your drafting approach and have adopted it. Your point that Katori's group also led early demonstrations and Ye's group also contributed to laser-coherence work is why I would not let the citation divide the credit. I also support your refusal to widen to a third name: another name would have to be justified by a decisive contribution that the evidence in front of us does not show, and ion-clock and comb contributions already have prizes. On the chair's question about recusal, I do not consider your stay in Hall's laboratory a trigger, since Hall is honoured for the comb and not for the lattice clock, and you report no tie to Katori or Ye. I would ask that it stay on the record.

uncertainties: Whether the committee as a whole accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes once the citation names the lattice clock explicitly; I think it does, but Olsson's consequence argument has not been fully answered.

The priority sequence between Katori's concept and the first lattice-clock demonstrations is recalled from general knowledge and not verified from documents, and the two-name credit rests on that recollection.
Whether the BHZ proposal was indispensable to the Molenkamp observation; if the committee concludes it was not, B007 would deserve a fresh look and my ordering could change.
Whether the pending SI redefinition should count as evidence of maturity; I treat it as coincident, but Lindroth and Kroll record that metrology prizes may be held back until it concludes.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or any other shortlisted name. My astroparticle and gamma-ray instrumentation experience (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+) and KTH collaboration ties are adjacent to B003, which I now list only as a later-year alternative, and I record no IceCube membership. As Chair I am both a participant in the leading position and the summariser of round 1, and I have tried to report the chair summary without weighting it toward B056. I see no recusal trigger for myself, and I do not advise recusal for Kroll on B056 on the basis of the disclosed Hall laboratory stay, while advising Johansson to abstain on B058.
